prior_narrative.tldr: This thread was regrouped from a broad 'large language models' reading list into reinforcement learning. Oct 15-23 papers centered on agentic RL environments, rollout budgets and credit assignment, with an AWS SageMaker guide for multi-turn RL.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 2-3: three more RL papers, including JHiMA-WebRL, a joint hierarchical multi-agent framework for long-horizon web tasks, and EffComp, which trains prompt compression with RL.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Nearly all of this is research: the recurring cost levers are rollout budgets, scheduling and credit assignment, which decide what agent RL training costs and whether it is stable.
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you train agents with RL, try rollout-budget or scheduling ideas on your own cost curve and rerun your evals; treat these preprints as unreplicated until code and independent results appear.

beats.summary: Training-stability and credit-assignment papers, plus AWS's hands-on multi-turn RL guide.

beats.headline: Calibration, error-targeted fixes, co-evolving harnesses and rollout scheduling
Self-learning, sequence confidence, skill routing, flow policies and causal explanations
Prompt compression, open multi-agent theory and hierarchical web agents
beats.summary: Nov 2-3: three more RL papers, ending with a multi-agent framework for long-horizon web tasks.

open_questions: Do rollout-budget and scheduling gains hold on production-size agent workloads?
Does fine-grained credit assignment help beyond the video-editing setting where it also hurt?
Will any of these frameworks ship code that others can reproduce?

storylines.label: Kimi K3.1
storylines.latest_title: Moonshot AI Publishes Kimi K3.1 Pro Weights on Hugging Face

prior_narrative.tldr: Kimi K3.1 started as a pre-release name tangled in China's proposed export-license rule, then was benchmarked against Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Moonshot launched K3.1 Pro on Oct 24, and a quota-driven rocky rollout was followed by third-party hosting.
prior_narrative.whats_new: vLLM shipped day-0 support for Kimi K3.1 Pro on Nov 4, and Verda opened a preview of its inference service serving the model the same day.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Self-hosting is now practical on vLLM, and K3.1 Pro is on several third-party clouds, so you can price it against first-party quotas, which Moonshot had to reset after launch complaints.

status.detail: K3.1 Pro has moved from a quota-troubled first-party launch to vLLM support and several third-party hosts; independent quality and cost data are still thin.

open_questions: Do independent evals show K3.1 Pro matching Opus 5.5 on coding or agent tasks?
What do third-party hosts charge versus Moonshot's first-party plans and quotas?
Does the proposed export-license rule restrict access to the open weights?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Pin the vLLM version before self-hosting K3.1 Pro and rerun your own evals against Opus 5.5 before changing routing. Keep a second host as fallback, since the first-party quotas failed at launch.

storylines.latest_title: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents?

prior_narrative.tldr: Reinforcement Learning is a loose grouping of agentic-RL papers, not one developing story. Since Oct 19 it has gathered research-state search training, memory-skill learning, and a study of when fine-grained credit assignment helps or hurts.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 3: MDSKILL, an arXiv paper, internalizes skill memory into agent weights through multi-view on-policy self-distillation, complementing RL for self-evolving agents.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Agent RL is shifting from prompt-held memory toward training signals: MDSKILL distills skill memory into the policy, and the Oct 26 credit-assignment study warns finer signals do not always help. All are paper-reported results, not production evidence.

status.detail: A loose set of agentic-RL papers; the newest moves skill memory from the prompt into the model via self-distillation.

beats.headline: ClueFlow trains long-horizon search on attributed research-state transitions
Lifelong agents learn memory and skills bidirectionally within a bounded context
Fine-grained credit assignment can help or hurt multimodal agents
beats.summary: Tested on video editing; finer credit is not automatically better.

beats.headline: CausalXRL explains RL decisions through causal graph reasoning
MDSKILL internalizes skill memory through multi-view self-distillation

open_questions: Does MDSKILL's internalized skill memory beat prompt-held skill memory on agent benchmarks beyond the paper's own?
Does ClueFlow's attributed research-state training carry to search agents outside the paper's benchmarks?
Do the credit-assignment findings from video editing hold on text-only tool-use agents?
Does bidirectional memory-skill learning stay stable over long interaction histories?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If you keep skill memory in prompts, rerun your evals against a distilled variant before committing, and A/B fine-grained credit against episode-level reward; treat all of these results as unreplicated.

prior_narrative.tldr: Early threads covered evaluating agent memory beyond the context window and invalidating stale entries (PACMI, Oct 5). On Oct 11 an open-source repo showed coding-agent memory as a tree of plain files.
prior_narrative.whats_new: ETAMem (Oct 27) splits heterogeneous memory types and aligns them for conversational agents, following ActionRAG (Oct 23), which retrieves relation-consistent evidence via graph diffusion.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Memory research is moving from simple stores to structured retrieval: relation-aware evidence (ActionRAG) and separated memory types (ETAMem). Both add moving parts you would have to run, test and version.

status.detail: Memory work now spans lightweight file stores and two new arXiv papers on structured retrieval; all are preprints or repos without independent replication.

beats.summary: Targets answers that depend on relations among facts, not isolated semantic matches.

open_questions: Does PACMI's invalidation cascade hold up on an independent long-horizon agent benchmark?

Do ActionRAG or ETAMem release code and benchmark numbers others can reproduce?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Before adopting a structured memory design, rerun it on your own long-conversation traces and compare against a plain retrieval baseline; both new papers are unreplicated preprints.

storylines.label: Typed Decision
storylines.latest_title: Presentation Sensitivity in Typed Decision Models for Subjective Text Evaluation

prior_narrative.tldr: Typed decision models return a probability over caller-defined options instead of generating text, and papers began placing them in agent systems as guardrails. The first paper showed an attack on that role; a security-triage study followed.
prior_narrative.whats_new: A paper on routing a personal multilingual inbox compares typed decision models against a classical baseline and a generative LLM, arguing to measure before training.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Typed decision heads are being proposed as guardrails and routers, so platform engineers need to know both how they can be attacked and how they compare with simpler baselines.

status.detail: Three papers in 15 days cover an attack, a security-triage application, and a baseline comparison for typed decision models.

beats.headline: Option-channel attack on typed decision guardrails
Typed, calibrated heads for perimeter triage
Measuring typed models against classical and generative baselines

open_questions: Do any vendors or papers publish defenses against the option-channel attack?
Do typed decision models hold their advantage over classical baselines on other routing tasks?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: If a typed decision model gates agent actions, test its option definitions for adversarial wording and benchmark it against a classical baseline before training.
